players.product: Mozaic HAMR nearline HDDs (44TB Mozaic 4+ -> 50TB Mozaic 5) for AI mass-capacity storage

quarterly_data.signal: HAMR QUALIFICATION BREADTH WIDENS BEYOND THE TWO LEAD CSPs (CFO Gianluca Romano): the 30 terabyte HAMR drive is now sold to 'all the hyperscalers in the world, all the big guys' and was qualified at the top 8, 10 customers in basically a year; the 40 terabyte drive is already selling to the two biggest hyperscalers in the world and is being qualified at 'a good number of customers, both in U.S. and in Asia', with more expected to qualify 'fairly soon'. All big customers are buying hundreds of thousands of HAMR units every quarter, and technology is 'not even a discussion with them anymore' - the discussion is capacity per unit (30 to 40 to 50). The 50 terabyte drive lands 'more calendar 2027 or through the end of calendar year 2027'.
quarterly_data.figure: 30TB qualified at top 8, 10 customers in about a year; 40TB shipping to the two biggest hyperscalers, qualifying at more customers in U.S. and Asia; hundreds of thousands of units per quarter

quarterly_data.signal: HAMR CROSSOVER AND THE END OF PMR IN THE DATA CENTER: management expects the HAMR volume crossover 'by December, so just a few months from now' for the 40 terabyte drive and for HAMR in general - the plan is 'really solid', with nothing pulling it in or pushing it out. In a couple of years, in the data center environment for Seagate, 80%-90% of the volume will be sold through HAMR. PMR cannot follow: 'you will not have a 50 terabyte drive, you will not have a 60 terabyte drive, you will not have a 70 terabyte drive' - above 30 terabyte, HAMR is the only solution, while PMR stays on the lower-capacity segments (Seagate sells hard disk drive from 2 terabytes to 40 terabytes today).
quarterly_data.figure: HAMR volume crossover by December; 80%-90% of Seagate data center volume on HAMR in a couple of years; PMR capped below 50 terabyte

quarterly_data.signal: INCREMENTAL GROSS MARGIN RUNNING FAR ABOVE THE INVESTOR-DAY FRAMEWORK: against the previously laid-out 50% incremental margin construct, management said recent quarters have been 'way higher than 50%... I would say in the 70-plus percent', and that 'for the next few quarters, I think that is a good way to look at the business'. Purchase orders are already in place for the entire fiscal year, on the basis of which Seagate sees every quarter of this fiscal year at higher revenue and higher margin; the pricing-plus-technology strategy has almost tripled gross margin over three years while Seagate remains 'low to middle single digit' of its customers' CapEx, which management argues makes further price increases sustainable.
quarterly_data.figure: incremental gross margin 70-plus percent vs the 50% framework; POs in place for the entire fiscal year

quarterly_data.signal: DEMAND IS ABOVE SUPPLY IN EVERY SEGMENT AND SEAGATE IS ALLOCATING: data center is about 80% of revenue (the big drives) and edge/IoT - consumer, client, part of video surveillance, drives of roughly 2 terabytes to 10, 12, maybe 14 - is 20%. 'Demand is above supply in every segment today', so Seagate allocates, giving priority to the big data center customers. In edge there are no purchase orders, no LTAs and no specific big customers, so Seagate changed its pricing strategy there in the last couple of quarters; high NAND pricing today is letting low-capacity HDDs take price while keeping volume 'fairly consistent'.
quarterly_data.figure: data center ~80% of revenue, edge/IoT 20%; demand above supply in every segment; edge drives 2 terabytes to 10, 12, maybe 14

quarterly_data.signal: LASER VERTICAL INTEGRATION IS SHIFTING THE HAMR HEAD BILL OF MATERIALS IN-HOUSE: the first generation of HAMR used only external lasers; with the second generation Seagate runs a mix, some products built with its internal laser and some still with external laser, and 'more and more we will go out in future, more the mix will go into the internal laser'. Producing the laser together with the head is 'much lower' cost than buying the laser outside and attaching it to the head later, with additional process and supply-chain risk benefits - a margin tailwind that grows with the HAMR mix.
